notes.front: Informal adjective: describes something suspicious, dishonest, or not quite right — not the smell of fish.
notes.example: The hotel keeps quoting me a different price — something's fishy.
notes.note: Idiomatic, not literal. Common frames: something's fishy, sounds fishy to me, a bit fishy.
notes.source: AEE #2653 — When Fishy and Cheesy Aren't About Food

notes.text: He said we could get rich overnight. That's already a red flag — sounds pretty {{c1::fishy}} to me.

notes.back: suspicious, dishonest, or not quite right
notes.example: "He suddenly changed his story." — "Yeah, it's a little fishy."

notes.front: Informal adjective: trying too hard to be funny or romantic; cliché, corny, a bit embarrassing.
notes.example: Did you hear his pick-up line? "Did it hurt when you fell from heaven?" So cheesy.
notes.note: Lighthearted, not usually offensive — but calling someone's heartfelt gesture cheesy can sting. Used of jokes, movies, pick-up lines, decorations, slogans.

notes.text: It was fun, but the decorations were a bit {{c1::cheesy}} — bright dollar-store stuff, not classy.

notes.front: What's the difference between calling something fishy vs cheesy?
notes.back:
fishy → suspicious / dishonest — you don't trust it.
cheesy → corny / cliché — trying too hard to be funny or romantic.
notes.example: "It's both fishy and cheesy — worst combo ever." (a scammy pitch that's also full of dramatic clichés)
notes.note: Both are food words used idiomatically, and both are casual/playful — great for connection.

notes.example: My husband was flabbergasted when he saw the henna sleeve.

notes.text: It's not really something that would be on his {{c1::radar}} — he'd never even thought about it.
notes.extra: on someone's radar = something they're aware of / paying attention to
notes.note: Opposite: fly under the radar = go unnoticed.

notes.text: The average parent has a few cheesy jokes up their {{c1::sleeve}}, ready for the right moment.
notes.extra: have something up your sleeve = keep it ready / in reserve (often secretly)

notes.front: Idiom: excessive, exaggerated, too much — done to a dramatic degree.
notes.example: The way he presented it was sort of over the top — all those dramatic lines.

notes.text: Anytime someone says you'll "get rich overnight," that's a red {{c1::flag}}.
notes.extra: a red flag = a warning sign that something is wrong

notes.front: Idiom: to consider feedback or a suggestion (politely) before deciding — you'll think it over, then do as you choose.
notes.example: I'll take all your feedback under advisement — and then do whatever I want.
notes.note: Slightly formal / tongue-in-cheek. Fixed phrase — note the preposition under.

notes.front: Noun (informal): someone who betrays your trust by telling on you, often to an authority figure.
notes.example: "I heard your brother told on you." — "Yeah, he's such a rat."
notes.note: Insulting. The whole family of expressions in this episode comes from this word.

notes.front:
Both mean "to tell an authority about someone's wrongdoing." What's the difference between
rat someone out and rat on someone?
notes.back:
No meaning difference — only the pattern differs:
• rat someone out — object goes in the middle: rat him out
• rat on someone — object follows: rat on him
notes.example: "She promised not to say anything, but then ratted me out." / "I wasn't planning to rat on him, but the boss asked me directly."
notes.note: Watch the word order — this is the trap for learners.

notes.text: Everyone agreed to stay quiet about the candy, but someone {{c1::ratted on}} us — the teacher knows.
notes.extra: rat on someone = tell on them to an authority

notes.text: I know, but who would {{c1::rat us out}}? We're still getting all our work done.
notes.extra: rat someone out = inform on them (object in the middle)

notes.front: Idiom: to suspect that someone is being dishonest or that something bad is secretly going on.
notes.example: Only a few people knew the plan, and now everyone does. I smell a rat.
notes.note: Related: have a rat = there's a traitor/leaker in the group.

notes.text: Someone must be leaking our strategies to our competitors — I think we {{c1::have a rat}}.
notes.extra: have a rat = there's a traitor/informant among us

notes.front: Childish noun + verb for someone who tells on others (playground register).
notes.back: a tattletale · to tattle on someone
notes.example: My daughter hits my son, then he's like "she hit me, she hit me!" — such a tattletale.
notes.note: Register: juvenile. Don't use about a coworker — say rat instead in adult/professional contexts.

notes.text: Scott's always giving us the {{c1::side-eye}} when we walk in late.
notes.extra: give someone the side-eye = a sideways look of suspicion or disapproval

notes.front: Idiom: the decisive factor between success and failure — it can determine everything.
notes.example: For a small business, the right hire can be make or break.

notes.front: Vocabulary map — name as many English expressions as you can for betraying trust / telling on someone.
notes.back: a rat ↔ rat someone out ↔ rat on someone ↔ tell on someone ↔ tattle / tattletale (childish) ↔ snitch ↔ smell a rat / have a rat (suspect a traitor)
notes.note: Register gradient: tattletale (kids) → rat / snitch (casual adult) → inform on someone (formal).
